Implement `src/sortBy.js`, a stable multi-key sort for arrays of records. A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

Ordering is locale-free. `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` all count as absent; absent values are equal to each other, and where they land is decided by `nulls` alone, never by `direction`, so `{ direction: 'desc', nulls: 'last' }` still puts them at the end. `compareValues` itself places absent values before every present value. A spec list that is not a non-empty array raises `TypeError` with message `at least one key spec is required`. goal.objective:
Implement `src/intervals.js`, a set algebra over half-open integer intervals. An interval is a two-element array `[start, end)` of safe integers that covers every integer x with `start <= x < end`. An interval list is normalised when it is sorted by start, contains no empty interval, and no two of its members overlap or touch: `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` touch and must coalesce into `[1, 5)`, while `[1, 3)` and `[4, 5)` must stay apart.

Export five functions. `normalize(intervals)` returns the normalised form of one list. `merge(a, b)` returns the normalised union of two lists. `intersect(a, b)` returns the normalised intersection; touching intervals share no integer, so `[1, 3)` against `[3, 5)` yields an empty list. `subtract(a, b)` returns the normalised relative complement `a \ b`. `coverage(intervals)` returns how many integers the list covers, counting an integer covered by several intervals once.

Every function validates both of its interval-list arguments before doing any work, and inputs may be adversarial: unsorted, duplicated, nested, negative, empty (`start === end`, which normalisation drops), or spanning a large range. A value that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `interval list must be an array`. A member that is not a two-element array raises `TypeError` with message `interval must be a two-element array`. A bound that is not a safe integer — a float, a numeric string, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or a value beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — raises `TypeError` with message `interval bounds must be safe integers`. An interval whose start exceeds its end raises `RangeError` with message `interval start must not exceed end`.

No function may mutate its arguments or return arrays that alias them; every returned interval is freshly allocated. `src/csv.js` must export `parse`, `stringify`, `escapeField` and the error class `CsvError`. `parse(text, options)` returns an array of records, each an array of field strings. A leading U+FEFF byte-order mark is dropped; anywhere else U+FEFF is ordinary data. Records are terminated by CRLF, LF or a lone CR, and a single terminator at the very end of the document closes the last record without starting an empty one, so `"a\n"` and `"a"` both read as one record while `"a\n\n"` reads as two and `"\n"` reads as one record holding one empty field. An empty document has no records at all. Fields are never trimmed, and an empty field is preserved wherever it appears, including at the start or end of a record.

A field is quoted only when the quote character is its very first character: there, the field runs to the matching closing quote, a doubled quote character stands for one literal quote, and delimiters and line terminators inside the quotes are data rather than separators. A quote character anywhere else in a field is ordinary text. After a closing quote only a delimiter, a line terminator or the end of the document may follow. `options.delimiter` (default `,`) and `options.quote` (default `"`) each take one UTF-16 code unit; they must differ from each other and neither may be a line terminator. `options.strictWidth` makes every record after the first have to match the first record's field count; without it ragged records are returned as they are.

Every failure throws `CsvError`. Positional failures carry a 1-based `line` and, where a single character is at fault, a 1-based `column` counted in UTF-16 code units from the start of that line: `unterminated quoted field` points at the opening quote, and `unexpected character after closing quote: b` points at the offending character, both accounting for line breaks that occurred inside a quoted field. `expected 2 fields, got 1` carries the line the offending record starts on. Bad arguments throw without a position: `input must be a string`, `delimiter must be a single character`, `quote must be a single character`, `delimiter and quote must differ`, `delimiter and quote must not be line terminators`.

`escapeField(value, options)` returns the text for one field. A string is used as it is; `null` and `undefined` become the empty field; booleans and finite numbers are converted with `String`; anything else throws (`unsupported field value: NaN` for non-finite numbers, `unsupported field type: object` otherwise). Reading a document this module wrote, with the same options, must return exactly the records it was given. Change only files under src/. Implement `src/sortBy.js`, a stable multi-key sort for arrays of records. A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

Ordering is locale-free. `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` all count as absent; absent values are equal to each other, and where they land is decided by `nulls` alone, never by `direction`, so `{ direction: 'desc', nulls: 'last' }` still puts them at the end. `compareValues` itself places absent values before every present value. Present values of the same type compare as follows: numbers numerically, with `-0` equal to `0`; strings by Unicode code point, so a code point above the basic plane sorts after `U+FFFD` and never by UTF-16 code unit, and never with `localeCompare`; booleans with `false` before `true`. Implement `src/intervals.js`, a set algebra over half-open integer intervals. An interval is a two-element array `[start, end)` of safe integers that covers every integer x with `start <= x < end`. An interval list is normalised when it is sorted by start, contains no empty interval, and no two of its members overlap or touch: `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` touch and must coalesce into `[1, 5)`, while `[1, 3)` and `[4, 5)` must stay apart.

Export five functions. `normalize(intervals)` returns the normalised form of one list. `merge(a, b)` returns the normalised union of two lists. `intersect(a, b)` returns the normalised intersection; touching intervals share no integer, so `[1, 3)` against `[3, 5)` yields an empty list. `subtract(a, b)` returns the normalised relative complement `a \ b`. `coverage(intervals)` returns how many integers the list covers, counting an integer covered by several intervals once.

Every function validates both of its interval-list arguments before doing any work, and inputs may be adversarial: unsorted, duplicated, nested, negative, empty (`start === end`, which normalisation drops), or spanning a large range. A value that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `interval list must be an array`. A member that is not a two-element array raises `TypeError` with message `interval must be a two-element array`. A bound that is not a safe integer — a float, a numeric string, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or a value beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — raises `TypeError` with message `interval bounds must be safe integers`. An interval whose start exceeds its end raises `RangeError` with message `interval start must not exceed end`.

Within a piece, runs of one or more spaces separate words and collapse to a single space; leading and trailing spaces disappear, and a piece with no words yields one empty line. A word wider than the column is broken greedily into chunks of at most `width` columns, so a 2-column character that would straddle the edge starts the next chunk and leaves the previous one a column short; a single character wider than the whole column throws `'UNWRAPPABLE'` with message `character is wider than the column`. Words and chunks are then packed greedily, one space between neighbours on the same line, starting a new line whenever the next word would push the line past `width`.

`padCell(text, width, align)` pads one already-fitting line to exactly `width` columns, with `align` defaulting to `'left'` and also accepting `'right'` and `'center'`; centring puts the smaller half of the padding on the left. It throws `'BAD_CELL'` for a non-string, `'BAD_WIDTH'` with message `width must be a positive integer` for a bad width, `'BAD_ALIGN'` with message `unknown alignment: <align>` for anything else, and `'CELL_TOO_WIDE'` with message `content is wider than the column` when the text does not fit. `formatTable(rows, options)` renders `rows`, an array of arrays of strings, using `options.widths` (an array of positive integers, one per column), the optional `options.align` (one alignment per column, all `'left'` by default) and the optional boolean `options.header`. Validation runs in this order, each failure throwing immediately: `options` must be a non-null object (`'BAD_OPTIONS'`, `options must be an object`); `widths` must be a non-empty array of positive integers (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `widths must be a non-empty array of positive integers`); `align`, when given, must be an array of the same length (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `align must have <n> entries`) holding known alignments (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `unknown alignment: <value>`); `rows` must be an array (`'BAD_ROWS'`, `rows must be an array`); and each row, in order, must have one cell per column (`'BAD_ROW_LENGTH'`, `row <i> has <n> cells, expected <m>`, counting a non-array row as 0 cells) with every cell a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell at row <i>, column <j> is not a string`). No rows renders the empty string. Otherwise every cell is wrapped to its column, a row occupies as many lines as its tallest cell with the shorter cells padded out with blanks, and the cells of one line are padded and joined with ` | `. When `header` is true a rule of hyphens per column joined with `-+-` follows the first row. Lines are joined with newlines, with no trailing newline, and every line of the result has the same display width. Change only files under src/.
